rows.title: Enhancement: Make shell completion descriptions use terminal width instead of fixed 45-character limit
rows.body:
---
  Enhancement: Make shell completion descriptions use terminal width instead of fixed 45-character limit
 📋 Current Behavior

  When generating shell completions, Click's get_short_help_str() method uses a hardcoded limit of 45 characters by default. This causes command descriptions to be truncated with ... even when there's plenty of terminal space available.

  Code reference: https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/main/src/click/core.py#L1097

```
  def get_short_help_str(self, limit: int = 45) -> str:
      """Gets short help for the command or makes it by shortening the
      long help string.
      """
```

  ---
  ❌ Problem

  Modern terminals typically have 80-200+ columns of width, but completion descriptions are limited to 45 characters. This truncation:

  - ❌ Cuts off important information that would easily fit
  - ❌ Creates a poor user experience in shell completion
  - ❌ Doesn't adapt to the user's terminal size
  - ❌ Feels dated compared to modern completion systems (zsh, fish, etc.)

  ---
  📸 Example

  With current 45-character limit

  Even with a terminal width of 150+ columns, completions are truncated:

  admin      -- Import bootstrap data, backup/restore...
  store      -- Import, export and bootstrap the knowledge...
  workspace  -- Import, export and reload the project...

  With terminal-aware limit

  The full descriptions would easily fit and be more informative:

  admin      -- Import bootstrap data, backup/restore workspace or get status.
  store      -- Import, export and bootstrap the knowledge graph store.
  workspace  -- Import, export and reload the project workspace.

  ---
  💡 Proposed Solutions

  Option 1: Use terminal width by default ⭐ (Recommended)

```
  def get_short_help_str(self, limit: int | None = None) -> str:
      """Gets short help for the command or makes it by shortening the
      long help string.
      """
      if limit is None:
          import shutil
          limit = shutil.get_terminal_size(fallback=(80, 24)).columns

      if self.short_help:
          text = inspect.cleandoc(self.short_help)
      elif self.help:
          text = make_default_short_help(self.help, limit)
      else:
          text = ""

      if self.deprecated:
          deprecated_message = (
              f"(DEPRECATED: {self.deprecated})"
              if isinstance(self.deprecated, str)
              else "(DEPRECATED)"
          )
          text = f"{text} {deprecated_message}" if text else deprecated_message

      return text.strip()
```

  Pros:
  - ✅ Adapts automatically to user's terminal
  - ✅ Backward compatible (just better defaults)
  - ✅ No breaking changes
  - ✅ Simple implementation

  ---
  Option 2: Add class-level configuration

```
  class Command:
      # Class-level default for completion descriptions
      completion_description_limit: int | None = None  # None = use terminal width

      def get_short_help_str(self, limit: int | None = None) -> str:
          if limit is None:
              limit = self.completion_description_limit
          if limit is None:
              import shutil
              limit = shutil.get_terminal_size(fallback=(80, 24)).columns
          # ... rest of implementation
```

  Pros:
  - ✅ Allows applications to customize behavior
  - ✅ More flexible for edge cases
  - ✅ Still maintains good defaults

  ---
  Option 3: At minimum, increase the default

  Change the default from 45 to 100 or 120 characters.

  Pros:
  - ✅ Easiest to implement
  - ✅ Minimal risk

  Cons:
  - ⚠️ Still doesn't adapt to terminal width
  - ⚠️ Still arbitrary

  ---
  🔧 Current Workaround

  Applications currently need to override Group.shell_complete() to work around this limitation:

```
  import shutil
  from click import Command, Context
  from click.core import _complete_visible_commands
  from click.shell_completion import CompletionItem

  class MyGroup(Group):
      def shell_complete(self, ctx: Context, incomplete: str) -> list[CompletionItem]:
          terminal_width = shutil.get_terminal_size(fallback=(200, 24)).columns

          results = [
              CompletionItem(name, help=command.get_short_help_str(limit=terminal_width))
              for name, command in _complete_visible_commands(ctx, incomplete)
          ]

          results.extend(Command.shell_complete(self, ctx, incomplete))
          return results
```

  This workaround:
  - Requires understanding Click internals
  - Must be implemented by every application
  - Duplicates code across projects

  ---
  ✨ Benefits

  - ✅ Better UX: More informative completion descriptions
  - ✅ Adaptive: Automatically uses available terminal space
  - ✅ Modern: Aligns with current shell completion standards
  - ✅ Universal: Benefits all Click-based applications
  - ✅ Compatible: Backward compatible with existing code
  - ✅ Simple: Applications passing explicit limit still work

  ---
  🔒 Compatibility Considerations

  The proposed changes are backward compatible:

  1. Existing code passing explicit limit parameter continues to work
  2. Code not passing limit gets better behavior automatically
  3. Fallback limit (80) ensures reasonable behavior in edge cases
  4. No API changes or deprecations needed

  ---
  🌍 Environment

  - Click Version: 8.x
  - Python Version: 3.8+
  - Shells tested: zsh, bash
  - Terminal widths tested: 80-200 columns

rows.title: Incorrect type annotation for `auto_wrap_for_ansi` in `_compat.py` causing type checking issues
rows.body:
**Bug Summary**
The type annotation for `auto_wrap_for_ansi` at line 15 of `click/src/click/_compat.py` is inconsistent with its actual function signature at line 522, causing type checking errors that require `# type: ignore` comments.

**Location**
- File: `click/src/click/_compat.py`
- Line 15: Incorrect type annotation
- Line 522: Actual function definition
- File: `click/src/click/utils.py` - Call site affected by the inconsistency

**Problem Details**
1. **Line 15 annotation**: `auto_wrap_for_ansi: t.Callable[[t.TextIO], t.TextIO] | None = None`
   - This suggests the function takes only one `t.TextIO` parameter
   
2. **Line 522 actual signature**: `def auto_wrap_for_ansi(stream: t.TextIO, color: bool | None = None) -> t.TextIO:`
   - The actual function takes two parameters: `stream` and an optional `color`

3. **Impact**: 
   - In `utils.py`, the call `file = auto_wrap_for_ansi(file, color)` requires `# type: ignore` to bypass type checking
   - This prevents proper type checking in the codebase
   - May confuse static type checkers and IDEs

**Expected Behavior**
The type annotation at line 15 should match the actual function signature, allowing proper type checking without the need for `# type: ignore` comments.

**Proposed Fix**
Change line 15 from:
```python
auto_wrap_for_ansi: t.Callable[[t.TextIO], t.TextIO] | None = None
```
to:
```python
auto_wrap_for_ansi: t.Callable[[t.TextIO, bool | None], t.TextIO] | None = None
```

**Additional Notes**
- After fixing the type annotation, the `# type: ignore` comment in `utils.py` can be removed
- This will improve code quality and enable better static analysis

rows.title: Support `OSC 9;4` in progress bar
rows.body:
`OSC 9;4` is a terminal feature that enables native (terminal) progress bar information. It supports various progress bar states and colors. There are various advantages to this system; one being that progress can still be displayed, even in a different tab.  

You can find some docs on this here https://conemu.github.io/en/AnsiEscapeCodes.html#ConEmu_specific_OSC or https://rockorager.dev/misc/osc-9-4-progress-bars/ (a really good post but the terminal support section is slightly outdated) 

When used, the sequence is consumed by the terminal and no text is displayed to the user. Meaning, this should be pretty lightweight to add to the logic where the progress bar is displayed.

One thing to note is that not all terminals do support this feature. More accurately, some older versions of the mainstream terminals do not support this feature. And so you might want to make this an opt-in feature. (Opt-in from the programmers side.) For example, iTerm2 only recently added support. But otherwise, it is supported in linux, macos, and windows.

A good place to get a good sense of the discourse around this feature request would be in pytest. The initial request https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/issues/13072 the request to make it opt in https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/issues/13896. Although, notably, iTerm2 does now support the progress bar too (the reason for the change to opt-in by pytest).

My main justification for adding this here, instead of a library that extends click, is similar to why pytest made it part of their core. (The first pytest link I sent has that convo.)

rows.title: `lookup_default` returns `Sentinel.UNSET` instead of `None`
rows.body:
Upgrading click to 8.3.0 or 8.3.1 causes a regression in lookup_default

# Reproduce

Change the click dependency in the below reproduce case to 8.2.1 and the assertion does not fail.

Install uv.  Run with `uv run repro_click_unset_regression.py` or simply `repro_click_unset_regression.py'.
 
```python
#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run
# /// script
# dependencies = ["click==8.3.1"]
# ///
"""
Run with uv installed:
  repro_click_unset_regression.py
Expected (pre 8.3.0): lookup_default returns the prefix-level default string or None.
Actual (8.3.0+): returns Sentinel.UNSET instead of None.
"""
import importlib.metadata
import sys
import click

class CustomClickContext(click.Context):
    def lookup_default(self, name: str, call: bool = False):
        if call:
            default = super().lookup_default(name, call=True)  # call: Literal[True]
        else:
            default = super().lookup_default(name, call=False)  # call: Literal[False]

        # Original logic (kept to reproduce): treats any non-None (including sentinel) as a real default.
        if default is not None:
            return default
        prefix = name.split("_", 1)[0]
        group = getattr(self, "default_map", {}).get(prefix)
        if group:
            return group.get(name)
        return default

def describe(value):
    cls = value.__class__
    return {
        "repr": repr(value),
        "type": f"{cls.__module__}.{cls.__qualname__}",
        "has_name_attr": hasattr(value, "name"),
        "name_attr": getattr(value, "name", None),
    }

def main():
    default_map = {"app": {"email": "prefix-param-level@example.com"}}
    cmd = click.Command("get-views")
    ctx = CustomClickContext(cmd, info_name=None)
    ctx.default_map = default_map

    val = ctx.lookup_default("email", False)
    info = describe(val)
    print(f"click version (importlib.metadata): {importlib.metadata.version('click')}")
    print("lookup_default raw:", info)
    # This assert fails under ≥ 8.3.0 because val is the internal Sentinel.UNSET object.
    assert val is None, (
        f"Regression: got {info['repr']} ({info['type']}) instead of expected builtins.NoneType"
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except AssertionError as e:
        print("AssertionError:", e)
        sys.exit(1)

```

# Expected
Return None instead of internal Sentinel.UNSET detail.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.14
- Click version: 8.30, 8.3.1

rows.title: Validate min <= max in `FloatRange` constructor
rows.body:
This feature should add a validation check to the `click.types.FloatRange` constructor.

When a `FloatRange` object is created, if both `min` and `max` are provided (are not `None`), the constructor should check if `min > max`. If `min > max`, it should immediately raise a `ValueError` or swap the `min` and `max`.

Currently, it is possible to create an invalid range:
```python
from click.types import FloatRange

# Problem: This is allowed, but creates an invalid state
# where min (0.0) is greater than max (-1.0)
invalid_range = FloatRange(min=0.0, max=-1.0, clamp=True)

# This invalid state leads to confusing behavior.
# A user might expect 0.0, but it clamps to the 'max' value (-1.0).
result = invalid_range.convert(0.0, None, None)
print(result)  # Output: -1.0

rows.title: `click.core.batch` loses elements when batch_size is larger than iterable length
rows.body:
The `click.core.batch` function appears to incorrectly handle cases where the provided `batch_size` is larger than the number of items in the iterable.
When the iterable is not empty but contains fewer items than `batch_size`, the batch function seems to return an empty iterator/list instead of a final, incomplete batch. This violates the invariant that the total number of elements processed by batch should equal the total number of elements in the original iterable.

```python
import click
from click.core import batch 
test_iterable = [0]
batch_size = 2

batched_result = batch(test_iterable, batch_size)

result_list = list(batched_result)

total_elements = sum(len(chunk) for chunk in result_list)

print(f"Click version: {click.__version__}")
print(f"Original iterable size: {len(test_iterable)}")
print(f"Batch size: {batch_size}")
print(f"Batched result: {result_list}")
print(f"Total elements processed: {total_elements}")


expected_result_list = [[0]]
expected_total_elements = 1

assert result_list == expected_result_list, \
    f"Expected {expected_result_list} but got {result_list}"

assert total_elements == expected_total_elements, \
    f"Expected {expected_total_elements} element(s) but got {total_elements}"

print("\nAssertion passed: Behavior is correct.")
```

```
AssertionError: Expected [[0]] but got []
```

Environment: Linux

- Python version: 3.12
- Click version: 8.3.0

rows.title: Add `CliRunner.set_filesystem()` to use a specific working directory
rows.body:
The `CliRunner.isolated_filesystem` is find for testing tools that have no preconceived notion of what the directory structure should look like, or what files must be present. While it's true that you can provide a parent directory to `isolated_filesystem()`, it will still create a brand new empty directory and operate within it.

`CliRunner.set_filesystem()` operates in the same way, except that you provide it with a pre-existing directory to operate in.

Suppose your tool requires that it be run in a directory named 'library' containing certain data files. Your test might look start like this:

```python
def test_library(tmp_path):
    lib_dir = tmp_path / "library"
    data_file = lib_dir / "data"
    lib_dir.mkdir()
    data_file.touch()
```

With `isolated_filesystem()`, running your command in this directory will not work, because it will run not in the library directory just created, but in a sub-directory of that one.

With `set_filesystem()`, you get what you need:

```python
    ...
    runner = CliRunner()
    with runner.set_filesystem(lib_dir):
        runner.invoke(...)
```

rows.title: Using a class as a `flag_value` causes the default to be instantiated in click 8.3.0
flag_value with default has undocumented ordering requirements in 8.3.0.
rows.body:
The 8.3.0 documentation section covering flag values (https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/options/#flag-value) currently has the following sample code:

```python
import sys

@click.command()
@click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default=True)
@click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')
def info(transformation):
    click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())
```

The code in this example works as documented, however there is an undocumented requirement: the option with `default=` set **MUST** be first for the code to behave as documented. In the sample code, moving the `--lower` option above the `--upper` option will break the documented behaviour.

The following two runnable scripts show the issue.

First, the version as documented:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import click

import sys

@click.command()
@click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default=True)
@click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')
def info(transformation):
    click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    info()
```
This gives the following output:

```
$ ./works.py --upper
LINUX
$ ./works.py --lower
linux
$ ./works.py
LINUX
```

Changing the order of the two `--upper` and `--lower` options:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import click

import sys

@click.command()
@click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')
@click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default=True)
def info(transformation):
    click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    info()
```

This gives the following output:
```
$ ./broken.py --upper
LINUX
$ ./broken.py --lower
linux
$ ./broken.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/venv/./broken.py", line 15, in <module>
    info()
  File "/tmp/venv/test/lib/python3.12/site-packages/click/core.py", line 1462, in __call__
    return self.main(*args, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/tmp/venv/test/lib/python3.12/site-packages/click/core.py", line 1383, in main
    rv = self.invoke(ctx)
         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/tmp/venv/test/lib/python3.12/site-packages/click/core.py", line 1246, in invoke
    return ctx.invoke(self.callback, **ctx.params)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/tmp/venv/test/lib/python3.12/site-packages/click/core.py", line 814, in invoke
    return callback(*args, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/tmp/venv/./broken.py", line 11, in info
    click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())
               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: attribute name must be string, not 'NoneType'
```

This ordering requirement either needs to be documented clearly, or fixed.

rows.title: New "default" behaviour in Click 8.3.x is broken for negative boolean flags
rows.body:
The behaviour of `default=...` for flag values changed in Click 8.3.0, as documented in [the release notes](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/changes/#version-8-3-0). The new behaviour is broken for negative flags, unless I am holding it wrong. Here's a minimal reproducer (put this in `foo.py`):

```python
import click

@click.command('foo')
@click.option('--without-xyz', 'enable_xyz',
              help="Disable xyz", flag_value=False, default=True, show_default=True)
def foo(enable_xyz):
    print(f'enable_xyz = {enable_xyz}')

foo()
```

The intent here is that we have an argument representing whether `xyz` is enabled, and a flag named `--without-xyz` which defaults to being disabled. Here, "disabled" means that the flag is *not* passed, which means the `default=True` value is used to initialize the `enable_xyz` variable. If `--without-xyz` were passed, the `flag_value=False` would be used to initialize `enable_xyz` instead, which makes sense. Or at least, that was the case in Click 8.2.x:

```
% ./foo.py
enable_xyz = True

 % ./foo.py --without-xyz
enable_xyz = False
```

However, with Click 8.3.0, `default=True` is now being treated as a special case. Special cases are often surprising, and indeed here this leads to the following behaviour:

```
% ./foo.py
enable_xyz = False

% ./foo.py --without-xyz
enable_xyz = False
```

I don't see how the new behaviour makes sense, at least for negative flags. I do not understand why a special case is needed for flags, as documented:

> But there is a special case for flags. If a flag has a flag_value, then setting default=True is interpreted as the flag should be activated by default. So instead of the underlying function receiving the True Python value, it will receive the flag_value.

Is there a reason for this special case?

FWIW, this is a pretty major breaking change that results in the negative flag being always unset. This will often result in a silent change in behaviour for software that used to work as intended. Such software may keep functioning (depending on what `--without-xyz` was disabling), but may change behaviour, performance characteristics, etc. This is pretty bad -- I would have much much preferred a loud error to this silent behaviour change.

Anyway, here are some thoughts:
- Is the special case really useful and necessary?
- Would it make sense to make this an explicit error instead of silently changing behaviour in Click 8.3.x?
- If the Click developers find that this is working as designed, what's the canonical way of adding options like `--without-xyz` that default to being "off"? This solution should not require flipping the logic of the application, i.e. using a `disable_xyz` variable name instead (which indeed simplifies the Click option definition but creates double-negatives in the user code that wants to check `if not disable_xyz`).
- Once the path forward is decided, I believe that a documentation update might be helpful to at least cover how negative options should be done.

Cheers and sorry in advance in case I missed something in the documentation that explains my confusion.

Environment:
- Python version: Python 3.10 (but it should reproduce anywhere)
- Click version: 8.3.x

rows.title: Suggest `Did you mean` for misspelled commands
rows.body:
### Summary

It would be useful to end users of click CLI applications if when they misspelled CLI sub-commands they got a helpful `Did you mean...` error message in a similar way to when they misspell an `@option` name (e.g., `--name`).

### Motivating Example

Consider the following example Click CLI app:

```py
import click


@click.group()
def cli():
    pass


@cli.command()
@click.option("--name", "-n", default="World")
def greet(name: str) -> None:

Misparsing of options passed after arguments when using group with invoke_without_command=True
rows.body:
When using `click.group(invoke_without_command=True)` with arguments and options, the parsing behavior differs depending on the order of arguments and options. It is incorrect when options are given after arguments.

Example:
```python
import click


@click.group()
def app():
    pass


# --- GOOD ---
@app.command(name="good")
@click.argument("name", nargs=-1)
@click.option("--greeting", "-g", default="Hello", help="Greeting word")
def good_greet(name, greeting):
    """
    This works fine with:
        python cli.py good alice bob --greeting Hi

    Result: Hi, ('alice', 'bob')!
    """
    click.echo(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

# --- BAD ---
@click.group()
def bad():
    pass

@bad.group(invoke_without_command=True)
@click.argument("name", nargs=-1)
@click.option("--greeting", "-g", default="Hello", help="Greeting word")
def bad(name, greeting):
    """
    This behaves differently with:
        python cli.py bad alice bob --greeting Hi

    Result: Hello, ('alice', 'bob', '--greeting', 'Hi')!

    However, works fine with:
        python cli.py bad --greeting Hi alice bob
    """
    click.echo(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

app.add_command(bad)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()
```

Expected Behavior:
Options should be parsed consistently regardless of whether they are provided before or after arguments.

Actual Behavior:
When `invoke_without_command=True` is set, options placed after positional arguments are treated as additional arguments instead of being parsed as options.

Steps to Reproduce

1. Run:
```bash
python cli.py bad alice bob --greeting Hi
```
2. Observe that --greeting Hi is incorrectly included in name.


Environment:
- Python version: `3.12.3`
- Click version: `8.3.0`

rows.title: WIP: Help page customization low level api
OSError: Windows error 6 when displaying error messages in Windows console
rows.body:
### Description:

Click applications fail with OSError: Windows error 6 when attempting to display error messages (like invalid options) in Windows PowerShell/Command Prompt. This appears to be related to Click's Windows console stream handling failing during exception display.

The error occurs in Click's exception handling code when e.show() tries to write error messages to stderr, which uses Click's Windows console wrapper that fails with "Windows error 6".

### Steps to Reproduce:

Create a Click CLI application with options
Install it as a Python package with an entry point
Run the application with an invalid option (e.g., --invalid-option)
Observe the OSError: Windows error 6 instead of a proper error message
Minimal Reproduction:

Create click_bug_repro.py:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import click

@click.command()
@click.option('--device-id', type=int, help='Device ID to use')
@click.option('--input-channel', type=int, default=0, help='Input channel')
def cli(device_id, input_channel):
    """Test CLI that reproduces the Windows console error."""
    click.echo(f"Device ID: {device_id}, Input Channel: {input_channel}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cli()
```
Create pyproject.toml:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=61.0", "wheel"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "click-bug-repro"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Minimal reproduction of Click Windows console bug"
requires-python = ">=3.8"
dependencies = ["click>=8.0.0"]

[project.scripts]
click_bug_repro = "click_bug_repro:cli"

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["."]
```

Then:

```shell
pip install -e .click_bug_repro --invalid-option
```

### Expected Behavior:

Should display a proper error message like:

```shell
Usage: click_bug_repro [OPTIONS]
Try 'click_bug_repro --help' for help.

Error: No such option: --invalid-option
```

Actual Behavior:

```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "click\core.py", line 1382, in main
    with self.make_context(prog_name, args, **extra) as ctx:
         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  ... (Click parsing the invalid option)
  File "click\exceptions.py", line 87, in show
    echo(f"{self.ctx.get_usage()}\n{hint}", file=file, color=color)
  File "click\utils.py", line 321, in echo
    file.write(out)  # type: ignore
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "click\_winconsole.py", line 205, in write
    return self._text_stream.write(x)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "click\_winconsole.py", line 190, in write
    raise OSError(self._get_error_message(GetLastError()))
OSError: Windows error 6

```

### Environment:

- OS: Windows 10/11
- Python: 3.12.10 (also affects 3.8+)
- Click: 8.3.0 (also affects 8.0.0+)
- Terminal: PowerShell 7.6.0-preview.4, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt
- Installation: Both regular pip install and editable installs affected

### Additional Context:

- The error occurs specifically when Click's exception show() method tries to write to stderr
- Setting NO_COLOR=1 or FORCE_COLOR=0 does not resolve the issue
- The issue appears to be in Click's Windows console stream wrapper failing during error output
- Some users report this affects Windows Terminal, PowerShell, and Command Prompt
- The issue may be related to Windows console handle management in Click's _winconsole.py

### Workaround:

Monkey patch Click's Windows console detection before importing Click:

```python
import click._winconsole
click._winconsole._get_windows_console_stream = lambda stream: None
click._winconsole._is_console = lambda f: False
```

### Impact:

This affects any Click-based CLI application on Windows when users provide invalid options, making the applications appear broken instead of showing helpful error messages.

rows.title: Help (--help) page customization high level design
rows.body:
# Intro

This is a possible high level design for help page(passing in --help) customization. I hope to come to an ideal design that supports the standard and advanced user. I will put together my thoughts then try to work with the community to improve it.

# Design

Help pages are basically an infinite space for customization with a large number of edge cases. The edge cases stem from the historical development of terminals and the very many shells and terminal emulators, each running on one or more operating systems. Because of this, I think Click should have 2 ways to generate help:

1. Help pages generated directly by Click. No formatting except line breaks and alignment. The focus is on displaying information. Basically the current help pages with a couple of more features. There is a lot of customization on the text displayed but no layout or otherwise formatting customization. 

2. Very low level and completely customizable. The intention is for terminal customization libraries like Rich to be able to directly send their primitives to the terminal while having access to as much information about the current invocation as possible. The hope is that some people will write nice plugins, and then most users can pick a plugin that caters to their sense of taste. 

# Advantages

- the potentially infinite space for customization is clearly bounded for the maintainers in a way that is easily communicated to users 

- the bounding frees Click maintainers to concern themselves with making a good CLI toolkit 

- The design also allows for explicit hooks for very dynamic help page customization.

# Possible implementation path:
- implement low level API 
- implement the standard help page on top of low level API 

# Downsides: 
- the default help page is a bit lackluster

rows.title: Bug: Optional value not optional anymore
rows.body:
### Outline

As stated in [official documentation](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/options/#optional-value): 
> Setting `is_flag=False, flag_value=value` tells Click that the option can still be passed a value, but if only the flag is given, the value will be `flag_value`.

Since 8.3.0 this doesn't work anymore, instead `SystemExit` with "Error: Option '--xyz' requires an argument." is thrown.

### Replication of bug

Example taken from documentation:
```python
@click.command()
@click.option("--name", is_flag=False, flag_value="Flag", default="Default")
def hello(name):
    click.echo(f"Hello, {name}!")
```

```shell
$ hello --name
Error: Option '--name' requires an argument.
```

### Expected behavior

The code example above should work as
```shell
$ hello --name
Hello, Flag!
```

It's not even working in the generated documentation anymore: while [documentation up to Sep, 10th](https://web.archive.org/web/20250910222023/https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/options/#optional-value) shows the expected and correct behavior, [current documentation](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/options/#optional-value) demonstrates the bug.

- Python version: 3.11
- Click version: 8.3.0

rows.title: Allow optional argument(s) to precede mandatory argument(s)
rows.body:
I would like to be able to define a command that takes two arguments, of which the _first_ is optional, like this:

```python
import click
@click.command()
@click.argument("foo", required=False)
@click.argument("bar", required=True)
def main(*, bar: str, foo: str | None = None) -> None:
    click.echo(f"foo={foo!r} bar={bar!r}")
if __name__ == "__main__": main()
```

This program behaves as expected when two arguments are provided, and the `--help` output of this program correctly reflects my intent:

```none
$ python3 test.py --help
Usage: test.py [OPTIONS] [FOO] BAR

Options:
  --help  Show this message and exit.
```

The error message when _no_ arguments are provided is also correct as is:

```none
$ python3 test.py
Usage: test.py [OPTIONS] [FOO] BAR
Try 'test.py --help' for help.

Error: Missing argument 'BAR'.
```

However, when only one argument is provided, it is assigned to 'foo' rather than 'bar' and so you get an error again:

```none
$ python3 test.py a
Usage: test.py [OPTIONS] [FOO] BAR
Try 'test.py --help' for help.

Error: Missing argument 'BAR'.
```

Instead, this invocation should set 'foo' to None and 'bar' to "b" and execute the command.

Note that click does currently support putting a _zero-or-more_ argument before a required argument, and this usage appears in the official [`inout` example](https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/main/examples/inout/inout.py), so I presume it's on purpose.  This slight variation on the example above works as expected:

```python
import click

@click.command()
@click.argument("foo", nargs=-1)
@click.argument("bar", required=True)
def fn(*, bar: str, foo: list[str]) -> None:
    click.echo(f"foo={foo!r} bar={bar!r}")

fn()
```

-->

```
$ python3 test2.py a
foo=() bar='a'
$ python3 test.py a b
foo=('a',) bar='b'
$ python3 test.py a b c
foo=('a', 'b') bar='c'
```

So, not being able to do the same with a _zero-or-one_ argument followed by a required argument seems inconsistent.

----

Here is an excerpt of help text for the program that motivated me to want this feature:

```none
mast-upload check-label [<label.yml>] <directory>

This mode assists you with the process of finalizing the label.
It checks for syntax errors, missing metadata, files in the data
set directory that aren’t covered by the label or explicitly marked as
excluded from the data set, files that don’t match what the label says
about them, etc.  Unlike `mast-upload scan` this mode will not modify
the label.  If you give only a directory on the command line, it will
look for `CONTENTS.YML` in the top level of the directory.
```

Putting the "label.yml" argument after the "directory" argument would confuse people into thinking that the _directory_ is being checked against the _label_, rather than the reality that the _label_ is being checked against the _directory_.

It is possible to work around the absence of this feature by shuffling parameters around after the fact in the command body:

```python
import click
@click.command()
@click.argument("bar_or_foo", metavar="[FOO]", required=True)
@click.argument("bar_or_none", metavar="BAR", required=False)
def main(*, bar_or_foo: str, bar_or_none: bar | None) -> None:
    if bar_or_none is None:
        foo = None
        bar = bar_or_foo
    else:
        foo = bar_or_foo
        bar = bar_or_none 
    click.echo(f"foo={foo!r} bar={bar!r}")
if __name__ == "__main__": main()
```

but this is fiddly and error-prone.

----

Right now, I only want this for programs which take exactly one or two command line arguments, of which the first is optional and the second is required.  A logical generalization would be to programs that take _one or more_ optional command line arguments, followed by _one or more_ required command line arguments.  The parser should count the actual number of non-option arguments supplied, issue an error if the count is less than the number of required arguments, fill in the required arguments left to right with the _last_ N non-option arguments, and then fill in the optional arguments left to right with whatever's left over.

Further generalization - to an arbitrary intermingling of required and optional - strikes me as undesirable, as the resultant CLI would be very confusing.  However, Click should _error out_ if the programmer tries to specify a mingled order, rather than generating a --help text that looks like nothing is wrong.

rows.title: `decorators.pyi` interface file?
rows.body: ### Background In [rich-click](https://github.com/ewels/rich-click) `1.9.0.dev1`, I added a `decorators.pyi` ([link](https://github.com/ewels/rich-click/blob/main/src/rich_click/decorators.pyi)) that enables typed args and-- critically for the developer experience-- tab completion for IDEs. So in rich-click, `@click.option()` (and other decorators) still take in arbitrary `**kwargs`, but as far as type-checking and the overall developer experience in a modern IDE is concerned, the experience is vastly improved: `context_settings=...` is an especially opaque and benefits tremendously from a `TypedDict`: ### The ask I've found this to be an incredibly useful change that vastly improves the developer experience, but I also feel like it should be something in base Click? It feels odd to add this additional functionality that's not in base click and is orthogonal to the purpose of rich-click, and yet it still feels like a necessity to have for modern development. **I'm posting this here because I am wondering if you are interested in a contribution to this effect.** I don't see any open issues relating to this. I would be willing to contribute this, especially since I've done a lot of this work already. ### Additional considerations - I think it is both a rare use case, and a violation of the Liskov substitution principle, to create a subclass of `Command`, `Option`, etc. that does _not_ accept all the parent class's args/kwargs. Additionally, if a user does this, then worst case scenario is they can just ignore their IDE's auto-completion, and the static type-checker also shouldn't get upset by it either. - `context_settings` takes in an arbitrary dict, but in rich-click's `decorators.pyi`, we use a `TypedDict`. I don't think it's common for developers to subclass `Context`, but it's certainly possible, and `Context` will often take in additional kwargs. Thus, if not handled properly, a `TypedDict` could cause a static type checker to fail when it shouldn't. Additionally, [PEP 728](https://peps.python.org/pep-0728/) is a long way's away. - That said, there is a simple solution: `@overload` the command and group decorators' `context_settings` to take in both a `TypedDict` and a `dict[str, Any]`; by placing the `TypedDict` as the first overload, PyCharm autocompletes correctly (this is untested with VSCode). as long as `cls=Command` or `cls=None` then the TypedDict is appropriate; otherwise for any arbitrary subclass of `Command` then an arbitrary dict[str, Any] is the appropriate type. - `core.py` would also strongly benefit from its own `core.pyi` because of the `Group.command` and `Group.group` decorators.

rows.title: Pager Popen() should not use `shell=True` now that the command is a list
rows.body:
In https://github.com/pallets/click/commit/299efb82e1a3d34d870129dc0c677c6efb42d811 a `Popen()` for the pager changed the command argument (the first argument) from a string to a list.

If changing the command to a sequence, we should also change `shell=True` to `shell=False` (or remove it).

Per the `subprocess` docs at

 * https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#popen-constructor

> On POSIX with `shell=True` … If _args_ is a sequence, the first item specifies the command string, and any additional items will be treated as additional arguments to the shell itself. That is to say, Popen does the equivalent of:
> `Popen(['/bin/sh', '-c', args[0], args[1], ...])`

Whereas if `shell=False` the effect is simply "`os.execvpe()`-like behavior" to execute `args[0]` directly with `args[1:]` as its arguments.

This bug is causing failures in the test suite for https://github.com/dbcli/mycli, and we are stuck on click < 8.1.8 as a result.

I don't have a prepared failure case using click other than the mycli test suite, but one example of strange behavior you can replicate easily is that `sh` will swallow arguments that you might think go to the command.  For example:

```bash
sh -c ls --nonsense
```

will work, because `ls` never sees `--nonsense`.

Environment:

- Python version: tested on Python versions 3.9-3.13
- Click version: 8.1.8+

rows.title: Support `FORCE_COLOR` and `NO_COLOR` environment variables
rows.body:
It would be great if the `FORCE_COLOR` and `NO_COLOR` environment variables could be used during calls to `click.echo`/`click.secho` to determine the default preference for colouring of stdout/stderr when an explicit preference for outputting colour is not set.

It appears that currently, click simply inspects whether the output stream considers itself to be a physical TTY. This is problematic on build systems such as GitLab or Jenkins or GitHub Actions, as logs that could be output in colour will not be since the output stream is still technically a file.

Supporting this would allow simpler catering for outputs that are designed to help visually impaired users when viewing automated build outputs, but may have other applications as well.

These environment variables are a good candidate to be used, because [the Python interpreter already considers these specific variables](https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#controlling-color), and other libraries such as `colorlog` also respect this.

rows.title: click.prompt and click.confirm argument prompt_suffix no longer works when suffix is empty
rows.body:
After #1836 and #2093 were merged the behavior of the `prompt_suffix` argument in the `click.prompt` and `click.confirm` functions changed.

# Before these changes in click version 7.1.2

Prior to the #1836 and #2093 PRs when an empty `prompt_suffix` was passed, no suffix was applied to the prompt.

Here's how `prompt` used to behave

```python
>>> import click
>>> click.prompt("test", prompt_suffix="")
testfoo
'foo'
>>> click.prompt("test", prompt_suffix=" ")
test foo
'foo'
```

Notice that when a `prompt_suffix of `""` is passed, there is no suffix after the prompt text of `test`. This is illustrated by how the text typed by the user (in this case `foo`) displays immediately after the prompt without a space character.

# Current behavior in click 8.0.0 and newer

```python
>>> import click
>>> click.prompt("test", prompt_suffix="")
test foo
'foo'
>>> click.prompt("test", prompt_suffix=" ")
test foo
'foo'
```

Notice now that if you tell `prompt` to use no suffix, it still applies a space character suffix.

This is because the fixes in #1836 and #2093 presumes that the last character of the prompt is a space character. It then [`rstrip`s the space character and adds the space character back in](https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/1836/files#diff-1f88635ce1d1f86bb7f9de29ef053bf8fc628a13530d1d2c6a69d0ad637e32cdR130-R133). This doesn't work if the last character of the prompt is not a space character though.

This matters because it makes it impossible to do prompts like the following example

# Example

```python
import click
click.prompt("What IP address would you like? : 192.168.1.", prompt_suffix="")
```

This would have the user enter the last octet of an IP and make it clear that they can only set something within the displayed subnet. The problem is that the resulting display looks like this

```
What IP address would you like? : 192.168.1. 123
```

# Note

The fixes in these two PRs can't just be reverted because the `readline` behavior that inspired them still exists.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13
- Click version: 8.0.3

rows.title: Improve text wrapping
rows.body:
[Currently click has 2 modes to display a help text](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/documentation/#escaping-click-s-wrapping):
1. Word-wrap the entire blob, and remove all other whitespaces
2. Preserve newlines, but disable word-wrapping


1) with a console width of 60, visualized with the `*`:
```
************************************************************
Usage: click_wrapping.py [OPTIONS]

Options:
  --test [value1|value2]  Example text to show word
                          wrapping. 'Value1' - short
                          comment. 'Value2' - A longer
                          comment that should wrap to the
                          next line.
  --help                  Show this message and exit.
************************************************************
```
2) with a console width of 60, visualized with the `*`:
```
************************************************************
Usage: click_wrapping.py [OPTIONS]

Options:
  --test [value1|value2]  Example text to show word wrapping.
                          'Value1' - short comment.
                          'Value2' - A longer comment that should wrap to the next line.
  --help                  Show this message and exit.
************************************************************
```

The 2nd option is slightly problematic, because on an actual console with width of 60, it looks like this:
```
************************************************************
Usage: click_wrapping.py [OPTIONS]

Options:
  --test [value1|value2]  Example text to show word wrapping
.
                          'Value1' - short comment.
                          'Value2' - A longer comment that s
hould wrap to the next line.
  --help                  Show this message and exit.
************************************************************
```

And that should probably be more along the lines of:
```
************************************************************
Usage: click_wrapping.py [OPTIONS]

Options:
  --test [value1|value2]  Example text to show word
                          wrapping.
                          'Value1' - short comment.
                          'Value2' - A longer comment that
                          should wrap to the next line.
  --help                  Show this message and exit.
************************************************************
```

Would a PR to fix this be accepted?
(As in, preserve newlines but still wrap on the console width)

rows.title: Impossible to get single newlines in help text
rows.body:
The expected format is:
```
  --annotations [disabled|comment]
                                  Specify the type of annotations to include in the XML output.
                                  'Disabled' - no annotations.
                                  'Comment' - annotations as comments.
```
The actual format is either:
```
  --annotations [disabled|comment]
                                  Specify the type of annotations to include in the XML output.

                                  'Disabled' - no annotations.
                                  'Comment' - annotations as comments.
```
or:
```
  --annotations [disabled|comment]
                                  Specify the type of annotations to include in the XML output. 'Disabled' - no annotations. 'Comment' - annotations as comments.
```



However the text either has _no_ newlines, or it has double newlines.
I expected this to work:
```python
@click.option(
    "--annotations",
    type=click.Choice(Annotations, case_sensitive=False),
    default=Annotations.Comment,
    help="""Specify the type of annotations to include in the XML output.
    \b
    'Disabled' - no annotations.
    'Comment' - annotations as comments.""",
)
```
But that ends up without any newlines.
Adding an extra blank line before the `\b` does work, but that also results in an extra blank line in the output (as seen above):
```python
@click.option(
    "--annotations",
    type=click.Choice(Annotations, case_sensitive=False),
    default=Annotations.Comment,
    help="""Specify the type of annotations to include in the XML output.

    \b
    'Disabled' - no annotations.
    'Comment' - annotations as comments.""",
)
```



Environment:

- Python version: 3.10.11
- Click version: 8.2.1

rows.title: Expanding args on windows must be changed
rows.body:
I have a tool which takes 3 parameters. 1 and 2 are of type str, the third is a Path. The second argument is a glob, that I give the tool to search stuff. This breaks everything, as click thinks it should expand that glob, no matter what I do - quotes, escapes, etc... nothing works.

## Example:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import click


@click.command()
@click.argument("stuff", type=str)
@click.argument("fileglob", type=str)
@click.argument("target_directory", type=click.Path(exists=True, dir_okay=True, file_okay=False, path_type=Path))
def tool(stuff: str, fileglob: str, target_directory: Path):
    print(stuff)
    print(fileglob)
    print(target_directory.as_posix())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tool()
```

<details>
<summary>Tests with the example</summary>

### Normal

```bat
python test.py abc **/*.zip C:\tmp
Usage: test.py [OPTIONS] STUFF FILEGLOB TARGET_DIRECTORY
Try 'test.py --help' for help.

Error: Invalid value for 'TARGET_DIRECTORY': Directory 'stuffff.zip' is a file.
```
### Quotes
```bat
python test.py abc "**/*.zip" C:\tmp                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
Usage: test.py [OPTIONS] STUFF FILEGLOB TARGET_DIRECTORY
Try 'test.py --help' for help.

Error: Invalid value for 'TARGET_DIRECTORY': Directory 'stuffff.zip' is a file.
```

### Escapes

> now this is a real fun one

python test.py abc "\*\*\/\*.zip" C:\tmp                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     16:52:31
Usage: test.py [OPTIONS] STUFF FILEGLOB TARGET_DIRECTORY
Try 'test.py --help' for help.

Error: Invalid value for 'TARGET_DIRECTORY': Directory '\\$Recycle.Bin\\S-1-5-21-220523388-115176313-1801674531-1814326\\$RO5LADT.zip' is a file.
```

</details>

## Expectation

I would expect the glob feature to only use non-quoted `Path` types and leave all the other arguments - *especially* str type args - alone.

rows.title: False "unexpected extra argument" error when Click group contains command named "list"
rows.body:
## Bug Description
  Click shows a false "Got unexpected extra argument" error when a Click group contains a command named `list` and another command uses `multiple=True` options with default handling. The error occurs even when no extra arguments are provided and the functionality works. correctly.

  ## Minimal reproduction case
  ```python
  #!/usr/bin/env python3
  import click

  @click.group()
  def cli():
      """Test CLI group."""
      pass

  @cli.command()
  def list():
      """This command causes the bug."""
      click.echo("List command works fine")

  @cli.command()
  @click.argument('name')
  @click.option('--format', '-f', 'formats', multiple=True, help='Formats')
  def run(name, formats):
      """This command shows false error when 'list' command exists."""
      # Set default format if none specified
      if not formats:
          formats = ('csv',)

      click.echo(f"Running {name} with formats: {list(formats)}")

  if __name__ == '__main__':
      cli()
```

  Command that triggers the issue

  python script.py run test

  Expected behavior

  Command executes without error messages:
  Running test with formats: ['csv']

  Actual behavior

  Shows false error but still executes correctly:
  Usage: script.py [OPTIONS]
  Try 'script.py --help' for help.

  Error: Got unexpected extra argument (csv)

  Root cause

  The issue appears to be a name conflict between the list command and Python's built-in list() function or Click's internal parsing logic.
   Renaming the command to anything else (e.g., list-reports, show) resolves the issue.

  Environment

  - Python version: 3.12
  - Click version: 8.2.1

  Additional notes

 The functionality works perfectly despite the error message - this appears to be a false positive in Click's error reporting system when parsing commands in groups that contain a command named list.

rows.title: Incorrect handling of quoted & escaped parameters for Fish completions
rows.body:
Completions for parameters in quotes, partially quoted or with escaped characters (e.g. whitespace) don't work properly for Fish shell.

I believe the issue is that for fish completion, the incomplete paramater is passed through the `COMP_CWORD` environment variable and it's expected that it will be contained in `COMP_WORDS` as the last parameter. However, before doing this match `COMP_WORDS` is parsed, which quotes and unescapes the parameters, while `COMP_CWORD` is not causing the match to fail. See code [here](https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/91ac02718af3a0b88dbe282501c06642da0785fe/src/click/shell_completion.py#L392).

## How to replicate

Consider the following command

```python
@click.command()
@click.argument('bar', type=click.Choice(('hello world',)))
def main(bar: str):
    pass
```

Trying to complete `foo hello` in Fish will correctly return completion for `foo hello\ world`.

The following incomplete commands will not return any completions
- `foo hello\ `
- `foo "hello`
- `foo "hello"`

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13.5
- Click version: 8.2.1

rows.title: `launch()` cannot locate files with spaces in the name on Windows
rows.body:
_Related to #2868 but with files and `locate=True`_

## Problem

When a Windows program uses `click.launch(some_path, locate=True)` and `some_path` contains spaces, then Windows Explorer opens showing the user's Documents folder and not the specified file.

Dispatching the call to `powershell` and not `cmd` seems to fix the problem.

## Reproduction

```pwsh
# Prepare and enter the virtual environment
mkdir click-demo
cd click-demo
python -m venv --upgrade-deps .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\activate.ps1

# Check versions
pip -V
# pip 25.1.1 from X:\scratch\click-demo\.venv\Lib\site-packages\pip (python 3.11)

# Install click
pip install click

# Check environment
pip list
# Package    Version
# ---------- -------
# click      8.2.1
# colorama   0.4.6
# pip        25.1.1
# setuptools 80.9.0
```

**`click-demo.py`**
```python
import pathlib
import subprocess

import click

# No spaces in this path
root_folder = pathlib.Path("C:\\Users\\Public")

# No spaces in this path
succeeding_folder = root_folder / "click-demo"
succeeding_folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
click.launch(str(succeeding_folder), locate=True)

# Path has spaces!
failing_folder = root_folder / "click demo"
failing_folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
click.launch(str(failing_folder), locate=True)

# Wrap with powershell
subprocess.run(
    [
        "powershell",
        "-Command",
        f"explorer /select,{failing_folder!s}",
    ],
    check=True,
)
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.11.9
- Click version: 8.2.1

rows.title: a race condition in `click.testing.StreamMixer`'s finalization
Add output of get_usage() to get_info_dict()
rows.body:
## Context 

I am generating some of my user-facing documentation using `get_info_dict()`, and was looking for a way to automate the usage as well without having to hardcode it in the docstrings. 

## Potential solution

Using the calls of `get_info_dict()` to add a `usage` key with the value being the output of `get_usage()`.

Other relevant issues: #2762 

## Workaround

For now I'm using `get_info_dict()`, then looping through the context to get groups and commands, and using `get_usage()` on each, then adding it to that dictionary. The code looks something like this (with the for loop matching the structure of my CLI):

```python
    info = ctx.to_info_dict()
    for cmd_n1 in ctx.command.list_commands(ctx):
        cmd2 = ctx.command.get_command(ctx, cmd_n1)
        sub_ctx = ctx._make_sub_context(cmd2)
        usage = cmd2.get_usage(sub_ctx).replace("Usage: ", "")
        info["command"]["commands"][cmd_n1]["usage"] = usage
        if isinstance(cmd2, click.Group):
            # Groups
            for cmd_n2 in cmd2.list_commands(ctx):
                cmd3 = cmd2.get_command(ctx, cmd_n2)
                sub_ctx3 = sub_ctx._make_sub_context(cmd3)
                usage = cmd3.get_usage(sub_ctx3).replace("Usage: ", "")
                info["command"]["commands"][cmd_n1]["commands"][cmd_n2]["usage"] = usage

```

rows.title: Drop `colorama`
rows.body:
We currently depend on [Colorama](https://github.com/tartley/colorama) on Windows, which converts ANSI formatting codes to equivalent Windows Console commands. However, on Windows >= 10, both the console host and Terminal app [support ANSI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/Microsoft.PowerShell.Core/about/about_ansi_terminals?view=powershell-5.1#ansi-terminal-support):

> On Windows 10 and higher, the Windows Console Host is [xterm](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Xterm) compatible. The [Windows Terminal](https://www.microsoft.com/p/windows-terminal/9n0dx20hk701) application is also xterm compatible. These terminals support ANSI escape sequences.

[Windows 10 reaches end of support on October 25, 2025.](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/end-of-support) We drop Python versions within 6 months of end of life, doing the same for Windows seems reasonable.

The last release of Colorama was October 24, 2022. [The year prior, they opened an issue explaining that maintenance was unlikely to move quickly, if it happened at all.](https://github.com/tartley/colorama/issues/300) This hasn't been updated since 2022 either.

Removing colorama would not break Click running on older versions of Windows. It would cause ANSI to be emitted unless `color=False` was passed to the context, which is easy enough to do if a project wants to opt-in to supporting older Windows versions.

rows.title: Add `help` to argument parameter
click.argument tilde gets expanded to "C:\Users\" on Windows
rows.body:
Hi! I believe click 8.0 introduced some strange behavior on Windows. A `click.argument` value that starts with a tilde (~) seems to get expanded into `C:\Users\`. At first I suspected it was the shell doing this expansion, but some tests show that `sys.argv` contains the correct non-expanded value, and testing Click 7.1.2 shows that the behavior started with version 8.0.0. This seems to only happen when the first character of the argument value is tilde.

Reproduction script:
```python
import click

@click.command()
@click.argument("arg")
def main(arg):
    click.echo(f"arg is {arg}")
    
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Test with click 7.1.2:
```
C:\Users\username> python repro.py ~hello
arg is ~hello
```

Test with click 8.2.0 (also 8.0.0):
```
C:\Users\username> python repro.py ~hello
arg is C:\Users\hello
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13.4
- Click version: 8.2.0

rows.title: No support for `python3.9` even though this is not EOL
rows.body:
We recently encountered some issues when doing a `pip install scancode-toolkit` due to some silent changes in how click handles ProgressBar attributes, i.e. `EnhancedProgressBar.is_hidden` was renamed to `EnhancedProgressBar.hidden`. Our CI was also failing because of this as we [test for latest versions of all dependencies](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/blob/develop/azure-pipelines.yml#L224) on supported OS/python combinations.

See https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/issues/4369 for more details on this.

We decided to use the new versions since we already had [complex version constraints](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/blob/develop/setup.cfg#L70) for click due to various regressions (like: https://github.com/pallets/click/issues/2832). We also [test for all click versions we support](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/commoncode/blob/main/azure-pipelines.yml#L61) to catch against regressions.

But this update does not work because starting click version 8.2.0, you are no longer supporting `python3.9` with https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/2893 

Note that because there was breaking changes and you've dropped a non-EOL python version simultaniously, we cannot use anymore latest versions of click going forward (or atleast untill python3.9 is EOL) since we plan to support using `scancode-toolkit` in all non-EOL python versions.

From https://palletsprojects.com/versions:
` it supports all Python versions that are not within six months of end of life (EOL)`

Seems like this change was introduced recently as [click 8.1.8 supported `python3.7`](https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/934813e4d421071a1b3db3973c02fe2721359a6e/pyproject.toml#L15) even though it was EOL for more than a year. While dropping support for EOL python versions is great and much welcomed, could you explain why you are dropping support for non-EOL versions since 6 months is a long time and as libraries we do need to support older python versions as they are still being used actively. IMHO being unable to use latest versions (with possible security updates) is worse than using non-EOL python versions.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.9
- Click version: 8.2.0 and above

rows.title: click.Choice now expects names instead of values for enums
rows.body:
Up until 8.1, options using `click.Choice` with a string enum would expect the enum value and return the corresponding enum instance. With 8.2, it now requires the enum name to be passed.

E.g. with the following code:

```python
from enum import StrEnum

import click


class Value(StrEnum):
    FOO = "foo"
    BAR = "bar"


@click.command()
@click.option("--value", type=click.Choice(Value))
def main(value):
    print(type(value), value)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

* click 8.1.0
```
$ python t.py --value bar
<enum 'Value'> bar
```
* click 8.2.0
```
$ python t.py --value bar
Usage: t.py [OPTIONS]
Try 't.py --help' for help.

Error: Invalid value for '--value': 'bar' is not one of 'FOO', 'BAR'.

$ python t.py --value BAR
<enum 'Value'> bar

```

This is a backward incompatible change.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.12.10
- Click version: 8.2.

rows.title: backspace and line-wrapping acting strange on Linux
rows.body:
When running any app using click.prompt on linux, something weird happens with backspace.

### Recording
This screen recording shows 2 letters being removed when I hit backspace once, and the prompt being deleted when I backspace the entire line.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dd505b9f-b412-49e0-aceb-d878cd291552)
([asciinema link](https://asciinema.org/a/qWORhMIcnEuG3iLtLvm9FwkhY))

The returned input is also different from the text shown on screen.

### Environment:

- Python version: 3.13.3
- Click version: 8.2.1


### Cause:

termui contains a workaround for windows where it prints a readline prompt itself. On linux, this confuses readline so things like backspace/ctrl-backspace and line wrapping don't work correctly.

This can be fixed by letting readline handling the prompt on linux: #2969

rows.title: Support for opposite of is_eager i.e. always process a parameter last
rows.body:
Hi,

Is there any way currently, or is there any appetite for a way to configure a parameter to always be processed last to work the opposite way to is_eager (is_uneager? is_apathetic? is_lethargic?).

I have a parameter that I would like to, when set, change the flow of the CLI command to instead open an interactive UI mode.

````
def run_ui(ctx, param, value):
    # open interactive ui

@click.command()
@click.option("--name", "-n", "name", required=True, default="Peter", help="Name of person to greet")
click.option(
        "--ui",
        is_flag=True,
        callback=run_ui,
        default=False,
        expose_value=False,
        help="Open the interactive UI mode.",
    )
def hello(name):
    #command logic
````

This interactive mode then gets pre-populated with any values already supplied via command line:
````
my_command hello --name Zoyd --ui # interactive mode will be populated with "Zoyd" rather than "Peter"
````

This works fine in the above case, but doesn't in the below:
````
my_command hello --ui --name Zoyd # --ui is processed before --name, so ctx doesn't include the name param
````

Is there any solution to this currently?

rows.title: Env var and flag options
rows.body:
Creating an `option` that `is_flag` and uses an `envvar` no longer works as expected, after version 8.2.0

This change was added:
https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/b63239d657aab7c4e04667a62e7177f617b37230/src/click/core.py#L2966

And documentation update says "if anything is defined in the envvar, the flag_value is returned, otherwise envvar value is" (latter being the old behavior)

Yet, it is IMPOSSIBLE to flag_value not set because it has always been set to something:
https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/b63239d657aab7c4e04667a62e7177f617b37230/src/click/core.py#L2613

This means I'm no longer able to use the document `ENVVAR=false` or `ENVVAR=0` because the new addition makes be "truthy" (`str("false")`)
Only setting `ENVVAR=` (empty value) will work.

Can we revert that?
Or update documentation properly (0, off, false, no longer valid false values).

rows.title: Support Enum values for token normalization
rows.body:
Click Choices uses Enum names instead of Enum values when normalizing. Enum values are more user-friendly than Enum names.

```python
class MyEnum(str, Enum):
   FOO = "foo-value"
   BIZ = "biz-value"
```

The command would look like:

```bash
my-command --choice foo-value
```

instead of

```bash
my-command --choice FOO
```

rows.title: CliRunner doesn't execute module code
rows.body:
When I use pytest with CliRunner it seems that the module code (before the entrypoint function) is not executed, or by the way something is missing.

Very ultra simplified example: I want an application which uses production or testing settings. The switch is done by an env variable. By default, I am using production settings

app.py
```python
import click
import os

print("IMPORTING SETTINGS")
print("MYAPPENV FROM GLOBAL: ", os.environ.get("MYAPPENV"))
settings_production = {"production": True}
settings_test = {"production": False}

# by default use production settings
settings = (
    settings_test if os.environ.get("MYAPPENV") == "testing" else settings_production
)

app = click.Group()


@app.command()
def main():
    print("Inside main command")
    print("MYAPPENV FROM MAIN: ", os.environ.get("MYAPPENV"))
    print(settings)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()
```

test_app.py
```python
from app import app
from click.testing import CliRunner

runner = CliRunner()

def test_app():
    result = runner.invoke(app, ['main'], env={"MYAPPENV": "testing"})
    print(result.stdout)
    assert False
```

If I run the application it works as expected. Output of python app.py main

```
IMPORTING SETTINGS
MYAPPENV FROM GLOBAL:  None
Inside main command
MYAPPENV FROM MAIN:  None
{'production': True}
```

as expected the global code is executed and we are in production=True. If I set the env variable to testing I get production=False, as expected.

```
# MYAPPENV=testing python app.py main

IMPORTING SETTINGS
MYAPPENV FROM GLOBAL:  testing
Inside main command
MYAPPENV FROM MAIN:  testing
{'production': False}
```

The problem is when I run `pytest test_app`: I get in the `Captured stdout call`

```
Inside main command
MYAPPENV FROM MAIN:  testing
{'production': True}
```

The expected behaviour should be exactly the one as when running the application with production=False, but

1) the global code seems not to be executed, at least I don't see the first printout
2) production is True, it should be False

rows.title: CliRunner does not flush stderr
rows.body:
`CliRunner` does not flush stderr as well, leading to `output` and `stderr` being empty if a `command` function prints to it and then exits.

Given the following script (I've tried my best to make it minimal):

```
import sys
from contextlib import contextmanager

import click
from click.testing import CliRunner


@click.group()
@click.option('-f', '--file', default=None, type=click.Path(file_okay=True))
@click.pass_context
def cli(ctx: click.Context, file):
    ctx.obj = {'FILE': file}


@contextmanager
def stream_file(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as stream:
            yield stream
    except OSError as exc:
        print(f"Error opening env file: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        exit(2)


@cli.command()
@click.pass_context
def list(ctx: click.Context) -> None:
    """Display all the stored key/value."""
    file = ctx.obj['FILE']

    with stream_file(file) as stream:
        print(stream)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    runner = CliRunner()
    result = runner.invoke(cli, ['--file', 'nx_file', 'list'])
    print(f"Stdout: \"{result.stdout}\"")
    print(f"Stderr: \"{result.stderr}\"")
    print(f"Output: \"{result.output}\"")
```

Running it with 8.2.0:
```
Stdout: ""
Stderr: ""
Output: ""
```

`stderr` and `output` should include the output from `print` in `stream_file`.

Running that same script with 8.1.8, which breaks because of 8.2 changes, but the output is still there.
```
Stdout: "Error opening env file: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'nx_file'
"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/steven/work/devel:languages:python/python-python-dotenv/cli.py", line 38, in <module>
    print(f"Stderr: \"{result.stderr}\"")
                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/tmp/tmp.WiykVOf20q/lib64/python3.11/site-packages/click/testing.py", line 150, in stderr
    raise ValueError("stderr not separately captured")
ValueError: stderr not separately captured
```

rows.title: `ParamType.get_metavar` has a new mandatory argument in 8.2.0
rows.body: I am using the `get_metavar` function to generate a custom metavar for some types. This was working fine, but upgrading Click to 8.2.0 broke our script. Unlike some other functions (e.g., `get_missing_message`), this is not even mentioned in the documentation that such a parameter was introduced. See ([docs link](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/api/#click.Choice.get_metavar)): Overall, such changes to the public documented API should not add mandatory parameters because that is adding breaking changes into a minor release. I get that this was added to enable a new feature, but I think you should consider using it as an optional parameter, which still adds a benefit of a new feature, while not introducing breaking changes to the public API. **Steps to reproduce:** 1. Use click 8.1.x 2. Call `get_metavar` to get some custom metavar (`get_metavar` has one parameter - `param`) 3. Update to 8.2.0 4. CLI crashes because a new mandatory parameter was introduced **Expected behavior:** No breaking changes to the public API in minor release, and better document the new parameter as you do for other functions. **Environment:** - Python version: 3.13 - Click version: 8.2.0

rows.title: Completion for commands in nested groups is broken in Click 8.2.0
rows.body:
## Summary

In Click 8.2.0, completion for commands in nested groups doesn't work as expected anymore. Instead of completing command options and/or arguments, completion infinitely repeats the command names for the group.

## Example program

Inspired by the example in #2847 

Save the following as `bin/nested` in a virtualenv

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

# nested

import click


def _complete_arg(ctx, _, incomplete):
    values = [
        "foo",
        "bar",
        "foobar",
        "baz",
    ]
    return [v for v in values if v.startswith(incomplete)]

@click.group
def main():
    ...

@main.group
def subgroup():
    ...

@subgroup.command
@click.option("--name", help="Name of something.")
@click.argument("arg", shell_complete=_complete_arg)
def compile(name: str | None, arg: str) -> None:
    """Test argument completion in nested groups."""
    click.echo(f"{name=} {arg=}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main.main()
```

Run `eval "$(_NESTED_COMPLETE=bash_source nested)"` to setup completion (for bash)

## Completion behavior

|Prefix|8.2.0 completion suggestions (unexpected behavior)|8.1.8 completion suggestions (expected behavior)|
|-|-|-|
|`nested`|`subgroup`|`subgroup`|
|`nested subgroup`|`compile`|`compile`|
|`nested subgroup compile`|`compile`|`foo     bar     foobar  baz`|
|`nested subgroup compile f`|none|`foo     foobar`|
|`nested subgroup compile --`|`--help`|`--name  --help`|
|`nested subgroup compile --name=n`|`compile`|`foo     bar     foobar  baz`|

## Environment

- Python version: Python 3.12.3
- Click version: 8.2.0

## Initial debugging

Reverting 0ef55fda47bb3d0dece21197d81d8d72a4250e73 for `src/click/shell_completion.py` restores the 8.1.8 completion behavior.

Looking at the change, I believe that the bug is actually caused by a simple statement reordering . IMO https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/af73ce4793bf38edf11a16e959ef0d8a0dbf6c1f/src/click/shell_completion.py#L567-L571 should be the following to preserve the 8.1.8 behavior:

```python
                    with cmd.make_context(
                        name, args, parent=ctx, resilient_parsing=True
                    ) as sub_ctx:
                        ctx = sub_ctx
                        args = ctx._protected_args + ctx.args
```

Note that Click 8.1.8 directly assigns `cmd.make_context()` to `ctx` in the equivalent snippet: https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/934813e4d421071a1b3db3973c02fe2721359a6e/src/click/shell_completion.py#L530-L531

In the same fashion, I believe that lines 589 and 590 should be switched in https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/af73ce4793bf38edf11a16e959ef0d8a0dbf6c1f/src/click/shell_completion.py#L581-L590

rows.title: Callback skipped on default value when command executed via forward() or invoke()
rows.body:
If a command is executed via `Context.forward()` or `Context.invoke()`, then any not-supplied parameters derived from options with both a `default` and a `callback` will not see their callbacks executed.

The following standalone demonstrates this:
```
import click
import datetime


@click.command()
@click.option("--date", type=click.DateTime(['%Y-%m-%d']),
              callback=lambda c, p, v: v.date(),
              default="2024-09-27",
              help="date on some calendar")
def hello(date: datetime.date) -> None:
    click.echo(f"Hello, world.  See you on {date.isoformat()}.")


@click.command()
@click.pass_context
def forwarding(ctx: click.Context) -> None:
    ctx.forward(hello)


@click.command()
@click.pass_context
def invoking(ctx: click.Context) -> None:
    ctx.invoke(hello)


@click.group()
@click.version_option(version="0.0.0")
def cli():
    pass


cli.add_command(hello)
cli.add_command(forwarding)
cli.add_command(invoking)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cli()
```

This is what I expected to happen:
```
$ python3 ./broken_forward.py hello
Hello, world.  See you on 2024-09-27.
$ python3 ./broken_forward.py forwarding
Hello, world.  See you on 2024-09-27.
$ python3 ./broken_forward.py invoking
Hello, world.  See you on 2024-09-27.
```

This is what actually happens:
```
$ python3 ./broken_forward.py hello
Hello, world.  See you on 2024-09-27.
$ python3 ./broken_forward.py forwarding
Hello, world.  See you on 2024-09-27T00:00:00.
$ python3 ./broken_forward.py invoking
Hello, world.  See you on 2024-09-27T00:00:00.
```

(The purpose of the callback on `--date` is to transform the `datetime.datetime` produced by `click.DateTime` into a `datetime.date`, as click has no built-in `Date` parameter type.  The two types have different `isoformat()` representations, so the failure to execute the callback is clear in the rendered output.)

Environment:

- Python version:  Python 3.13.3
- Click version:  8.1.8

rows.title: Click 8.2.0 ignores is_flag options that have a type
rows.body:
Click 8.2.0 ignores the use of options defined with `is_flag` and `type=str`.

Of course, combining `is_flag` and `type=str` does not make sense, but it happened in one of our projects. Click before 8.2.0 ignored `type=str` and processed this as expected for `is_flag`.

Click 8.2.0 does not set a value for such an option.

I could trace this change to PR #2829 - If I install click 8.2.0 and manually undo the change in `core.py` that is done by that PR, it works as before.

To reproduce:

1. Have a file `main.py` with:

```
import click

@click.group(invoke_without_command=True)
@click.option('-x', '--transpose', type=str, is_flag=True,
              help='Transpose the output table.')
def cli(transpose):
    print(f"Debug: transpose={transpose}")
    return 0
```

2. Reproduce with click 8.2.0:
```
$ pip install click==8.2.0
$ python -c "import main,sys; sys.argv=['cli', '--transpose']; main.cli()"
Debug: transpose=None
```

3. Verify that click 8.2.0 with PR #2829 undone works:
```
# perform the undo in core.py (see below)
$ python -c "import main,sys; sys.argv=['cli', '--transpose']; main.cli()"
Debug: transpose=True
```

4. Verify that click 8.1.8 works:
```
$ pip install click==8.1.8
$ python -c "import main,sys; sys.argv=['cli', '--transpose']; main.cli()"
Debug: transpose=True
```

The "undo" of PR #2829 has the following changes in `core.py`, starting at line 2613:
```
        # Undo PR 2829: Added the following two lines
        if flag_value is None:
            flag_value = not self.default
        self.type: types.ParamType
        if is_flag and type is None:
            # Undo PR 2829: Removed the following two lines
            # if flag_value is None:
            #     flag_value = not self.default
            # Re-guess the type from the flag value instead of the
            # default.
            self.type = types.convert_type(None, flag_value)
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.12.7 on macOS (it happens on all Python versions supported by click 8.2.0, but not on all OSs)
- Click version: 8.2.0

Based on our CI test run, the issue happens only on macOS and Windows, but not on Ubuntu: 
https://github.com/zhmcclient/zhmccli/actions/runs/14949544297. I did not investigate why it does not happen on Ubuntu.

The fix for projects using click is of course to remove `type` when `is_flag` is used.

Even though this is basically an incorrect use of click, I would expect click to surface this as an incorrect use, instead of silently not setting a value for the option.

rows.title: Add help string formatters that don't use escaped characters.
rows.body:
I'd love to use the `\f` and `\b` in my docstrings to have a single source of help text. However, [Ruff D301](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/escape-sequence-in-docstring/)  enforces [PEP 257](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/#what-is-a-docstring) which requires docstrings to be raw (`r"""…"""`) if they have any backslashes in them. Doing _that_ breaks the VS Code syntax highlighting to no longer treat the string as a docstring.

So, I've had to move documentation out of the docstring for the function and into the `help` argument, repeating the docstring first line, all because I want to use `\b` and `\f` to fight Click's helpful auto-formatting. Please add an additional formatting mechanism to support these functions. If I'm going to put visual garbage in my source file to get the formatting to behave, it would be nice if it were self-documenting, e.g. 

```python
@click.option(…)
@click.option(…)
def myfunc(cats: int = 0, feet: int = 0) -> None:
    """Does good stuff.
    
    Here's more detailed information
    on how this works.
    
    <<click-preserve-whitespace>>
    Examples:
         # basic usage
         $ myfunc
    
         # overrides
         $ myfunc --cats 1 --feet 17

    <<click-end-help>>

    Args:
        cats: Number of cats to assume prowling around.
        feet: How far cats can jump during attacks.
    """
    pass
```
